drills.q: Someone proposes running etcd with 4 nodes instead of 3 'for extra safety.' What's wrong with this reasoning?
drills.a: Quorum = floor(n/2)+1. 4 nodes need 3 to agree, tolerating exactly 1 failure — identical fault tolerance to a 3-node cluster, which also needs only 2 for quorum and tolerates 1 failure. The 4th node adds replication/storage/fsync cost with zero additional resilience. Go to 5 (tolerates 2 failures) if more fault tolerance is actually needed.

drills.q: Two clients both GET the same object, both compute an update, both PUT. What determines who wins and what does the loser see?
drills.a: Optimistic concurrency via resourceVersion. The first write to reach the API server succeeds and bumps the version in etcd. The second write's PUT carries the now-stale resourceVersion it originally read, so the API server rejects it with HTTP 409 Conflict — the client is expected to re-GET current state and retry its logic, not blindly resubmit.

drills.q: The API server starts rejecting all writes cluster-wide with 'mvcc: database space exceeded.' Walk through diagnosis and fix.
drills.a: etcd's backend size quota (default 2GB) was exceeded and it entered an alarm state. First investigate why the DB grew that large (commonly unbounded Events or high CRD churn), not just raise the quota. Fix: compact old MVCC revisions to free logical space, then defragment to actually reclaim disk space at the storage engine level — compaction alone doesn't shrink the on-disk file.

drills.q: A pod is Pending, kubectl describe shows '0/12 nodes are available.' How do you find the actual blocking constraint instead of guessing?
drills.a: Read the FailedScheduling event's per-reason breakdown line (e.g. '3 Insufficient cpu, 5 node(s) didn't match node affinity, 4 node(s) had taint...') rather than treating the summary as one undifferentiated failure. This tells you exactly which Filter plugin eliminated which nodes and points to the right fix (capacity vs affinity vs taint).

drills.q: Your custom controller is generating unusually high API server write load with no obvious external trigger. What's the most likely self-inflicted cause?
drills.a: Reconcile is calling Status().Update() (or any Update) unconditionally on every invocation instead of checking whether the computed value actually differs from current state. Since a status write is itself an object change, it generates a new watch event that re-enqueues the object, calling Reconcile again — an infinite self-triggering loop. Fix: semantic deep-equal check before writing.

drills.q: You scale your custom operator to 3 replicas for HA and start seeing intermittent conflicting writes to the objects it manages. First thing to check, and what if that checks out fine?
drills.a: First check whether leader election is enabled and functioning (a Lease object should show exactly one current holder) — without it, every replica reconciles independently and races. If leader election is confirmed correct and conflicts persist, look for a separate external writer: a human running kubectl edit/patch directly, a second controller with overlapping ownership, or a CI/CD pipeline applying colliding manifests — leader election only prevents the operator's own replicas from racing each other.

drills.q: kubectl delete on a CRD instance hangs indefinitely in Terminating state. Diagnose and describe the risky last-resort fix.
drills.a: A finalizer is present in metadata.finalizers and the owning controller either isn't running or is erroring on the cleanup path, so it never removes the finalizer. Check controller logs for the reconcile error. Risky last resort: manually patch finalizers to an empty list to force deletion — this should be understood as accepting orphaned external resources (whatever the finalizer's cleanup was supposed to do never happens), a workaround for a bug, not routine practice.

drills.q: A teammate wants to build a CRD and controller for a feature that's really just 'apply this ConfigMap and Deployment with slightly different values per team.' Is this justified?
drills.a: Generally no — a CRD-and-controller pair is a new permanently-running distributed system requiring its own monitoring and on-call, and the honest bar is whether it encodes real operational knowledge (failover logic, external resource lifecycle) a simpler tool can't express. Templating (Helm/Kustomize) covers 'apply with different values per team' without the ongoing controller maintenance burden. This is the operator-sprawl anti-pattern.

drills.q: Explain why Kubernetes controllers are described as 'level-triggered, not edge-triggered,' and what concrete guarantee this gives up in exchange for what benefit.
drills.a: Level-triggered means Reconcile reacts to 'something changed, go figure out what's currently true' by re-deriving from current observed state, rather than reacting to a specific event delta. It gives up the efficiency of precise incremental updates, but gains correctness under at-least-once delivery, dropped/coalesced events, and controller restarts with no memory — since correctness only depends on being able to observe current state and re-derive the right action, not on perfectly replaying a history of events.
